newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-BHP to tackle copper costs.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-BHP to tackle copper costs.

text.p: The Broken Hill Pty Co Ltd (BHP), facing criticism about the wisdom of its US$2.4 billion takeover of Magma Copper, expressed confidence on Wednesday that it could rope in runaway production costs.

The assurance helped lift BHP's share price above the A$16.00 level for the first time this week and appeared to signal the temporary end of harsh comment by brokers and investors that one of Australia's best known and biggest companies had paid a top-of-the-cycle price for the U.S.-based mining and smelting operation.
BHP shares gained 28 cents to end local trade at A$16.20, tracking a recovery in most mining stocks as overnight base metal prices improved.

The company's embattled managing director, John Prescott, told reporters that while production costs had soared since BHP bought Arizona-based Magma in January, this problem would be tackled as a priority.

After being told last week that Magma lost money in the 1996/97 first quarter (June/August), disgruntled shareholders were told on Tuesday at the BHP annual meeting that Magma's production costs had jumped to about 85 U.S. cents a pound to match the current spot price, meaning the operation was only a break-even proposition.
This production cost compared with 68 U.S. cents when the takeover was completed.
"There's some one-offs in there that we need to address and there's no doubt that we can improve on the 85 cents," Prescott said.
"It's not as if there's some fundamental weakness in the Magma business. The basis is there for a strong performance for BHP," he said.

BHP last Friday reported a disappointing first quarter net profit of A$287 million in the three months to August 31, compared with A$372 million a year ago, due largely to a slump in profits from its copper division.
While every effort would be made to fix problems at Magma, Prescott could not say when it would return to profits.
"Hopefully what we've seen is an aberration rather than a continuing thing," he said, adding he did not know what copper prices would do.
"They are at a very low level. I don't think they're going to go up a lot in the near term."
"A turnaround is certainly achievable," said Peter O'Connor, an analyst for Macquarie Equities Ltd, said of the Magma outlook.

By world standards, analysts say an average production cost of 68 U.S. cents is high, while 85 cents is deeply troubling, particularly given the mid-year collapse of the international copper market in the wake of the Sumitomo Corp trading scandal.
The benchmark copper sales price is only about 86 cents presently, down from around US$1.15 at the start of the year.
BHP's other major copper mines, the Escondida mine in Chile and Ok Tedi in Papua New Guinea produce copper for 40 U.S. cents or less per pound, casting a shadow over Magma.
Elaine Prior, an analyst at McIntosh Securities, said costs at these mines are lower because the ore bodies are richer and there is more associated gold in them than at Magma.
